title: Up the mountain (Matthew 5:1–2)
hook: he sits down, the way a rabbi teaches, and opens his mouth

segments.voice: Yesterday, beginning, back to Galilee, and your line was start again, knowing more. Now camp five: the depths.

A speaker stops pacing. Pulls up a chair. Sits down. The room goes quiet, because something is about to be said. The path now goes somewhere new: the Sermon on the Mount, chapters five, six and seven of Matthew's Gospel. A long block of Jesus's teaching, full of lines people still quote, often without knowing where they come from. Blessed are the meek. Turn the other cheek. Salt and light. The Lord's Prayer. Treasure where moth and rust corrupt. The house on the rock. And Matthew sets the scene in just two verses.
screen: `A SPEAKER SITS DOWN.` → `MATTHEW 5 TO 7.` → `LINES PEOPLE STILL QUOTE.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in the King James Bible: "And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him: And he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying." Three small details, each one doing something. First, he went up into a mountain. Some readers hear an echo of Moses, who went up Sinai and came down with the law: here's a new teacher on a mountain, giving teaching about how to live. Matthew never names the mountain. Tradition places it on a hillside above the Sea of Galilee, near Capernaum, and a church stands there today. Second, when he was set: when he sat down. Today a speaker stands to show authority. In his world, a teacher sat. Jesus sits down in the synagogue at Nazareth to teach, and later speaks of teachers who sit in Moses' seat. Sitting down means class is in session. Third, he opened his mouth. It sounds redundant; how else would he speak? But some readers hear a solemn way of saying, what follows is weighty, like saying, and he began. Luke has a shorter version of some of the same teaching, set on a level place, and some readers think Jesus taught these sayings more than once. Either way, the posture is the point. Before the disciples hear a single word, they come close. The sermon's first move isn't doing anything. It's coming near and listening.
screen: `HE WENT UP INTO A MOUNTAIN.` · `WHEN HE WAS SET: HE SAT DOWN.` · `HE OPENED HIS MOUTH.` · `THE DISCIPLES CAME NEAR.` · then, large: `AND HE OPENED HIS MOUTH, AND TAUGHT THEM.`

segments.voice: Sit, if you're not already, let your feet rest on the ground, and put your phone face down. For these two minutes, don't answer, fix or plan anything; just listen, to the room, to your breath, to what's underneath the noise. If you pray, you can come near, the way the disciples did, and let God speak first.
Moses, the echo some readers hear: as he went up Sinai, Jesus goes up a mountain too, and sits down the way a teacher did.
Your line: sit down, listen. The first words of the sermon come next. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Parts of the Sermon on the Mount come up in church readings through the year, and some Christians read all three chapters at once, slowly, as a whole.

fork.setup: you're one of the disciples. a crowd is gathering, and Jesus goes up the hillside and sits down. what do you do?
fork.reveal: "when he was set, his disciples came unto him." the sermon begins with coming near and listening.

original.note: Greek: mountain, hill. Matthew 5:1, he went up into a mountain.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Sermon on the Mount was a speech to a crowd.
what it means: Jesus sits down, as a teacher did, and his disciples come near, with the crowds listening.
what a scholar hears: some readers hear Moses on Sinai in Matthew's mountain; Luke 6 sets similar sayings on a level place.
recall: the disciple who denied Jesus three times
father, the word a child uses at home

notes: Camp open: camp five, the depths; part open: the Sermon on the Mount (days 232–261).
The Moses/Sinai echo is a widely held reading of Matthew; phrased as 'Matthew seems to want that echo'. Confirm.
Mount of Beatitudes near Capernaum/Tabgha, with a 20th-century church: 'a church stands there today'. Confirm.
'He opened his mouth' as a solemn idiom: a common commentary claim; confirm.
Relationship of Matthew 5–7 and Luke 6 is presented without choosing a theory.
